text:
I bought the Corvid Q3 mostly on a whim, after my third pair of budget wireless cans in four years gave up in the same spot: the left hinge. At $149, the Q3 sits in that awkward middle band where you're paying enough to expect competence but not enough to demand excellence. Having lived with them for six weeks, I can report that they mostly deliver, with one significant exception.

Let's start with the sound, because that's the exception, and I'd rather you hear it now than three paragraphs in. The Q3's tuning is aggressively consumer-oriented: boosted bass, slightly recessed mids, and a top end that gets sparkly in a way that veers toward harsh on poorly mastered tracks. If your library is mostly pop, hip-hop, and EDM, you'll probably love it. Kick drums hit with genuine authority, and the low-end extension is better than anything else I've heard at this price. But acoustic material suffers. Female vocals sit a beat behind the mix, and cymbals on older rock recordings take on a metallic edge that had me reaching for the EQ. The companion app offers a five-band equalizer and a handful of presets, and after some tinkering I landed on a setting that tamed the worst of it, but I shouldn't have to fix a company's tuning choices for them. If neutral reproduction matters to you, keep looking.

Everything else about these headphones is a pleasant surprise. Comfort, first. The Q3 weighs 248 grams, which is on the lighter side for over-ears, and the clamping force is calibrated almost perfectly: firm enough to stay put during a jog, gentle enough that I've worn them through two transatlantic flights without hot spots. The ear pads are a protein leather that breathes better than most, though I noticed some moisture buildup after hour four, which is typical for closed-back designs at any price. The headband cushioning is thin but well-placed. My only real complaint is that the cups don't fold flat, which makes them bulkier in a bag than they need to be.

Battery life is the standout. Corvid claims 55 hours with ANC off and 38 with it on, and my testing bore those numbers out almost exactly: I averaged 36 hours per charge with noise cancellation active, measured across five full discharge cycles with a mix of music, podcasts, and video calls. Five minutes of USB-C charging buys about four hours of playback in a pinch. There's also wireless charging via a pad on the right ear cup, a feature I initially dismissed as gimmicky but now use nightly, just setting the headphones down on my nightstand charger. I wish more manufacturers did this.

The active noise cancellation itself is mid-tier. It handles low-frequency drone well, clipping the rumble of airplane engines and train carriages down to a distant hum. Higher frequencies leak through: keyboard clatter and nearby conversation remain audible, just softened. The transparency mode is genuinely good, with a natural timbre and only slight artifacts in wind. Call quality is fine, nothing more. Colleagues reported I sounded "like a headset," which is to say clear but tinny.

Connectivity was flawless over six weeks. Multipoint pairing works exactly as advertised: I kept them connected to my laptop and phone simultaneously throughout, with clean automatic switching on incoming calls. Bluetooth 5.3, aptX Adaptive, and SBC are supported; iPhone users get AAC. Range held up across two rooms and a floor.

Which brings us to value. At $149, the Q3 competes against established players' older models and newcomers' loss leaders. It beats most of them on battery and comfort, loses to a few on sound refinement. The two-year warranty, including the ear pads, is generous for this bracket, and replacement parts are sold directly rather than locking you into a whole-unit replacement cycle.

Verdict: the Corvid Q3 is a very good pair of headphones with mediocre tuning. If you listen loud, bass-forward, and on the move, buy them without hesitation. If you sit still and listen closely, spend your money elsewhere. Three and a half stars out of five.
